summary.title: Inhibitor of sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase impairs paramyxovirus replication
summary.authors: Naveen Kumar, Sanjay Barua, Nitin Khandelwal, Kundan Kumar Chaubey, Ram Kumar, Krishan Dutt, Yogesh Chander, Thachamvally Riyesh, Vir Shoor Singh, Bhupendra Nath
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the role of sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase (SERCA) in paramyxovirus replication, specifically focusing on Peste des petits ruminants virus (PPRV) and Newcastle disease virus (NDV). The authors demonstrate for the first time that SERCA is a critical host factor facilitating paramyxovirus replication. Using the SERCA-specific inhibitor Thapsigargin, they show that treatment at non-cytotoxic concentrations significantly reduces viral replication in Vero cells. Conversely, overexpression of SERCA2 rescues the inhibitory effect of Thapsigargin, confirming SERCA's supportive role. The study reveals that paramyxovirus infection induces SERCA expression, which can be blocked by Thapsigargin. Mechanistic investigations using time-of-addition and virus step-specific assays indicate that Thapsigargin primarily inhibits viral entry and disrupts the subcellular localization of viral proteins, causing them to remain in cytoplasmic foci rather than localizing to the cell surface for budding. Notably, the study reports a rare phenomenon where NDV, but not PPRV, acquires significant resistance to Thapsigargin after long-term passage (70 passages) in Vero cells. This suggests that viruses may evolve to bypass dependency on cellular factors targeted by inhibitors. The findings highlight SERCA as a potential novel target for broad-spectrum antiviral therapeutics, offering a strategy to combat viral resistance by targeting host factors rather than viral proteins. The work contributes to the understanding of paramyxovirus replication mechanisms and the development of host-directed antiviral strategies.

claims.description: NDV can acquire resistance to SERCA inhibitors.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the role of sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase (SERCA) in paramyxovirus replication, specifically focusing on Peste des petits ruminants virus (PPRV) and Newcastle disease virus (NDV). The authors demonstrate for the first time that SERCA is a critical host factor facilitating paramyxovirus replication. Using the SERCA-specific inhibitor Thapsigargin, they show that treatment at non-cytotoxic concentrations significantly reduces viral replication in Vero cells. Conversely, overexpression of SERCA2 rescues the inhibitory effect of Thapsigargin, confirming SERCA's supportive role. The study reveals that paramyxovirus infection induces SERCA expression, which can be blocked by Thapsigargin. Mechanistic investigations using time-of-addition and virus step-specific assays indicate that Thapsigargin primarily inhibits viral entry and disrupts the subcellular localization of viral proteins, causing them to remain in cytoplasmic foci rather than localizing to the cell surface for budding. Notably, the study reports a rare phenomenon where NDV, but not PPRV, acquires significant resistance to Thapsigargin after long-term passage (70 passages) in Vero cells. This suggests that viruses may evolve to bypass dependency on cellular factors targeted by inhibitors. The findings highlight SERCA as a potential novel target for broad-spectrum antiviral therapeutics, offering a strategy to combat viral resistance by targeting host factors rather than viral proteins. The work contributes to the understanding of paramyxovirus replication mechanisms and the development of host-directed antiviral strategies.

Research Context
Antiviral strategies have traditionally targeted essential viral proteins. High mutation rates in viral genomes lead to drug resistance. This resistance has prompted a shift toward targeting host factors. Host factors can be proviral or antiviral. SERCA regulates calcium uptake into the endoplasmic reticulum. The role of SERCA in virus replication was previously unknown. Recent studies suggest other calcium ATPases support virus replication.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to determine if SERCA regulates paramyxovirus replication. The hypothesis is that SERCA facilitates viral entry and protein localization. It is predicted that inhibiting SERCA will reduce viral titers. Overexpression of SERCA is expected to rescue viral replication. The study investigates whether viruses can acquire resistance to SERCA inhibitors. It is hypothesized that NDV may develop resistance upon long-term passage.

Methodological Details
Vero, 293T, HeLa, and goat kidney cells were used. Cells were grown in DMEM with 10% fetal bovine serum. PPRV and NDV were used as the viral models. Thapsigargin was used as the SERCA inhibitor. Cytotoxicity was assessed using the MTT assay. Antiviral efficacy was measured by plaque assay at MOI 0.1. Virucidal activity was tested by incubating virions with Thapsigargin. Time-of-addition assays were performed to identify inhibited viral steps. SERCA2 overexpression was achieved using pCR3-SERCA2 plasmids. Immunofluorescence assays were used to visualize viral protein localization. Viral resistance was selected by 70 passages in Thapsigargin.

Procedures And Architectures
Thapsigargin was applied at 0.5 µM, a non-cytotoxic concentration. Virus titers were determined by plaque assay. For entry assays, preattached virus was allowed to enter at 37°C. Immunofluorescence involved fixation with 4% paraformaldehyde. Cells were stained with primary and secondary antibodies. Resistance selection involved sequential passage in 0.25 µM Thapsigargin. Virus harvest times varied between 72-120 hours for passage. Western blotting was used to analyze SERCA2 expression levels. GAPDH was used as a housekeeping control.

Key Results
Thapsigargin did not affect cell viability at concentrations up to 2 µM. Thapsigargin significantly inhibited NDV and PPRV replication. Thapsigargin did not exhibit virucidal activity on cell-free virions. Overexpression of SERCA2 rescued the inhibitory effect of Thapsigargin. PPRV infection induced SERCA2 expression at 3 hpi. Thapsigargin blocked virus-induced SERCA2 expression. Highest inhibition occurred when Thapsigargin was added 30 min pre-infection. Thapsigargin did not affect viral attachment, RNA synthesis, or budding. Thapsigargin treatment reduced NDV and PPRV entry. Defective subcellular localization was observed in ~70% of treated cells. NDV acquired significant resistance to Thapsigargin at passage 35. PPRV did not acquire resistance to Thapsigargin after 70 passages.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
SERCA is a crucial host factor for paramyxovirus replication. SERCA inhibition primarily impacts viral entry and protein localization. Targeting host factors may provide broad-spectrum antiviral activity. Viruses can acquire resistance to host-targeting agents. NDV resistance suggests a change in host factor requirement. SERCA is a potential candidate for antiviral drug development.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study could not determine direct interaction between SERCA and viral proteins. Co-immunoprecipitation assays were unsuccessful. The mechanism of NDV resistance is not yet understood. Fluctuations in viral titers occurred during passage experiments. The study did not identify specific viral mutations conferring resistance.

Claims
SERCA facilitates paramyxovirus replication. Overexpression of SERCA2 rescued Thapsigargin inhibition. Thapsigargin reduced viral titers. Thapsigargin did not affect viral attachment. SERCA is a potential antiviral target.
NDV can acquire resistance to SERCA inhibitors. NDV showed significant resistance at passage 35. PPRV did not show resistance. Complete resistance was not achieved. Viruses can evolve to bypass host factor dependency.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Control-passaged viruses did not exhibit resistance. Resistance was specific to Thapsigargin passage.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows Thapsigargin cytotoxicity and antiviral efficacy. Figure 2 shows SERCA2 overexpression rescues replication. Figure 3 shows virus-induced SERCA2 expression. Figure 4 shows time-of-addition assay results. Figure 5 shows Thapsigargin inhibits viral entry. Figure 6 shows defective subcellular localization. Figure 7 shows selection of resistant mutants.

Three Takeaways
1. SERCA is a critical host factor for paramyxovirus replication. 2. Thapsigargin inhibits viral entry and protein localization. 3. NDV can acquire resistance to SERCA inhibitors.
